en: Preface to the Direct Explanation of the Phonetic Glosses for the Newly Carved *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Now, the *Vajracchedikā* is that which elucidates the wondrous mind of humanity. As for this mind: it is brilliantly radiant and spiritually luminous, its light swallowing the universe;

it is profound, empty, and exquisitely pure, its illumination traversing as many worlds as grains of sand. It extends vertically through the three periods of time, such that even empty space cannot rival it.
Pervading the ten directions and encompassing heaven and earth, how could anything equal its vastness? Spanning from antiquity to the present, it is neither old nor new;
abiding among the holy and the ordinary, it neither increases nor decreases. This is the blissful land of all Buddhas and the fundamental source of all sentient beings.
Were it not for Subhūti, who could have investigated and clarified this profound doctrine? Were it not for Ānanda, who could have compiled these teachings? The scripture is divided into three parts.
The twelve divisions of the teachings, their various meanings, and the syllables of awakening—these five thousand words and more, word for word, all return to the Prajñāpāramitā.
The stages of the three vehicles and four fruits are all realized and established based upon this mind;
the diverse categories of the nine realms and four modes of birth all branch out from this principle. This sutra alone is most concise in its phrasing, yet its meaning is profound.
Though many may read deeply, those who awaken to it are few; once awakened, the head is no longer like that in a mirror, and upon waking, the pearl is found within one's own clothing.
It is as if a destitute son sees his father, or precious jewels appear before him in their full splendor;
or as when a madwoman sees her child, her frantic anxiety suddenly ceases. For those wishing to cross over, this is a great vessel; for those seeking peace, this is the true lotus.

Having read this work thoroughly, I have finally investigated its meaning. Drawing from various scriptures, I have provided a direct interpretation of this sutra, eliminating redundancy and prioritizing simplicity so that those who recite it may easily understand it;
I have led from the shallow to the profound so that students may enter its depths.
Aware that the sin of such audacious appropriation cannot be avoided, I have truly composed this for the benefit of those who uphold and maintain it.
Preface to the Carved *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
That which is the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle was taught by the Buddha for the sake of the Great Cause and Condition.
It serves as a mirror for the times and a scale for all things; just as one clears turbid water, one should employ the wondrous pearl of Bodhi.

To sever delusive dust, one must rely upon the adamantine jeweled sword; though the world comprises the distinctions of the three thousand great chiliocosms, a single thought-moment encompasses it all.
Sentient beings follow diverse paths—the nine types and ten classes—but they are all delivered toward the One True Reality.
This sutra is most concise, yet its principle is most profound. Those who recite it today merely seek blessings and virtue, rather than investigating the nature of those blessings.

The nature of virtue is thus. This new commentary on the text is titled *Zhijie* (Direct Explanation); as I am about to peruse it, I feel a sense of awakening and begin to believe that my humble understanding is not so far from the truth.
Water has not yet entered the sea, and thus it cannot become salty; a person has not yet investigated principle, and thus how could they reach the source of the mind?
Alas! The purport is profound and the Way is subtle; how could those of shallow insight believe in this? Only those of superior wisdom know it.
As a fine horse sees the whip, the gate of Nirvana is near; as an inferior person hears it, they are like a foolish monkey grasping at the moon. How vast indeed is the path of birth and death!
O elder brother who bears the burden of Heaven, having heard this sutra, you have provided the funds for its carving and printing to bestow it upon those with aspiration so they may behold it.
If one can attain awakening through a single word, what need is there to endure the delusions of kalpas? Do not accept further merit and virtue [for this].
How could one sink into the sea without knowing that dharmas are without self? Only by realizing non-arising can one find the source by tracing the current;
only by understanding the scriptures can the fundamental tenets be clarified. Now that Master Gaoming has provided this commentary, I, Yuan, have also composed this preface for it.
Direct Explanation and Phonetic Glossary of the Newly Carved *Mahāyāna Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
by the Monk Yuangao of Chenggao in the Sixteen Celestial Caverns of Wuyi. Commentary and Notes.
Seng Yuanyan, Proofreader; Yunqing’an;
Seng Yuanlu; Seng Yuangui. Invocation for the Embroidered Edition of the Diamond Sutra.
If there are those who read and recite this sutra, they must single-mindedly distance themselves from all miscellaneous thoughts and thoroughly investigate the meaning of the sutra.
First, one should contemplate the mantras for purifying body and speech; thereafter, one should invoke the names of the Eight Vajras and the Four Bodhisattvas.
Thus, wherever one may be, one will always receive protection.
The Mantra for Purifying the Body:
*sūtari sūtari sumarī svāhā*. The Mantra for Purifying the Karma of Speech.
Svāhā to the Earth-Deity Mantra: Namo samantabuddhānām | Oṃ dhuru dhuru dharidhi svāhā.
The Mantra of Universal Offering: Oṃ gagaṇasvabhāva-vajra hoḥ. Vajra.
I invoke the Vajra of Blue Disaster-Dispelling; I invoke the Vajra of Poison-Averting;
I invoke the Vajra of Yellow Wish-Fulfilling; I invoke the Vajra of White Pure Water;
I invoke the Vajra of Red Sound; I invoke the Vajra of Holding Stability and Dispelling Disaster.
I respectfully invoke the Vajra of Purple Wisdom; I respectfully invoke the Great Deity Vajra;
I respectfully invoke the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi; I respectfully invoke the Bodhisattva Vajrapāśa.
I respectfully invoke the Bodhisattva Vajraprīti; I respectfully invoke the Bodhisattva Vajrabhāṣa.
The commentary states: These eight Vajras and four Bodhisattvas were originally a *caṇḍāla*—here translated as "butcher"—during the time of the previous Buddha Kāśyapa.
He happened upon a scroll of the *Sūtra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas* before a temple and took it home with him.
Through the merit of his offerings, he was moved by a divine response: his wife became pregnant and gave birth to a mass of flesh. Upon cutting it open, he found eight boys;

their hearts were upright and righteous, their strength surpassing that of men, and they were able to subdue all who were wicked and evil. Later, his wife again gave birth to a mass of flesh; upon cutting it open, there were four girls;
their countenances were dignified and beautiful, their kindness and compassion excelled the multitude, and they observed the fasts and honored the Buddha.
The transformed elder brother left the household life, and the twelve siblings together took refuge in Kāśyapa Buddha to practice and protect the Teaching.
The men attained the stage of Vajra-holders and the women attained the stage of Bodhisattvas; because they constantly protect this sutra, they are stationed before it.
If anyone recites this sutra and earnestly entreats them, these Vajra-holders and Bodhisattvas will provide protection wherever they may be.
Vow Text: I bow my head to the Honored One of the Three Realms; I take refuge in the Buddhas of the ten directions.
I now make this great vow to uphold this Diamond Sutra, To repay the fourfold heavy恩情 (en) above, And to deliver those suffering in the three miserable realms below.
If there are those who see or hear [this], may they all resolve their minds on Bodhi; at the end of this present physical existence, may they be born together in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
What is "Brahman"?
How does one attain long life and a vajra-like indestructible body?
By what causes and conditions does one obtain great, firm, and solid strength? How does one reach the ultimate further shore regarding this sutra?

We pray that the Buddha will reveal its subtle and profound mysteries and explain them extensively for the sake of all sentient beings. (This sutra was divided into thirty-two sections by Prince Zhaoming of the Liang Dynasty.)
The Verse for Opening the Sutra:

The unsurpassed, most profound, and subtle Dharma, Difficult to encounter in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas— I have now seen, heard, received, and upheld it; May I understand the true meaning of the Tathāgata.

In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "Vajra" (Diamond) is a metaphor for the true essence of the mind. The essence of a person's mind is like refined gold that has been smelted a hundred times.

Just as gold does not diminish its essential nature even after being smelted a hundred times, and its golden color remains unchanged even when fashioned into various vessels, so too is the human mind.

The essence is likewise so: though intermingled with various conditions, the spirit and mind remain unclouded; though mixed among the multitude of categories, the substance of the mind remains eternally numinous.
Therefore, the mind is as eternally firm as empty space, and like gold, it remains ever-refined through the ages. Thus, the mind is compared to gold.
"Hardness" is a metaphor for the true wisdom of the mind. A person's mental wisdom is like a sharp-edged blade of steel;
though the blade cuts through myriad things, its substance remains ever-hard. Even after being polished a thousand times, the blade's edge becomes even sharper. Mental wisdom is likewise.
The wisdom that discerns all objects remains ever-clear as the eye of wisdom; it comprehends all phenomena while the mind of wisdom is eternally tranquil.
Thus, wisdom possesses the capacity for decisive judgment, just as a blade has the function of cutting and severing. This is why wisdom is likened to a sharp sword.
*Prajñā* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "wisdom. Wisdom is the true discernment of the mind. The light of wisdom is like a mirror:

when various forms approach the mirror, their beauty and ugliness manifest spontaneously within its reflection. Just as no form, whether minute or vast, remains hidden in a mirror’s clarity, so it is with the wisdom of the mind:
it can illuminate the most obscure and know the most subtle; there is no dust that does not appear before it, and no object that remains unperceived.
It is not manifest. Wisdom possesses the clarity of foresight, and a mirror possesses a body of penetrating brilliance; therefore, wisdom is compared to a mirror.
*Pāramitā* is a Sanskrit term; in this [language], it means "reaching the other shore. "Shore" refers to land. It is divided into "that" [shore]...
Therefore, there are this shore and the other shore. This shore is the delusion of the mind. It moves upon encountering conditions; it arises upon perceiving objects.
Whenever one encounters objective conditions, various deluded phenomena arise. All those with karmic conditions transmigrate on this shore.
This is merely the land where sentient beings receive retribution for their karmic consciousness. When the karma of sentient beings is exhausted, this shore...
It has been extinguished. That which is the "other shore" is the fruit of the mind. The numinous void is revealed alone; it is tranquil, pure, and profoundly still.

It cannot be defiled by dust nor conditioned by dharmas; it is the land of the person who has attained the fruit. When the mind is ever perfectly luminous, profound, and still, this is itself the other shore.
The Sūtra is the path of the mind. If a person practices according to this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, they will reach the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Viewed in this light, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is—
This is precisely the single true mind of each person. If one is deluded by it, birth and death begin; if one awakens to it, saṃsāra ceases.
Now, the practitioner who knows this self-mind wisdom understands that this self-nature is truly without delusion.
Using the lamp of wisdom to illuminate and shatter worldly conditions, they comprehend these illusory phenomena and establish the myriad practices without attachment.
Regarding the mind: when encountering various conditions, the mind remains ever serene and still. Practicing in this manner, one swiftly ascends to the other shore.
A verse says: The meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is manifold; Only with a raft can one cross the river.
If the mirror of the mind is not yet clear, do not be indolent; One must further undergo refinement through study and practice.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yaoqin, under imperial decree.
Yaoqin was a puppet king of the Eastern Jin; his surname was Yao and his name was Xing, and he served as the King of Qin. As for "Tripiṭaka": it refers to...
These are the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras. Kumārajīva—translated as "Child-Longevity" (Tóngshòu)—is so called because he possessed the talents and virtue of an elder even while still a child.
Thus, the King of Qin issued an edict for the translation of this scripture; a translator is one who renders the Sanskrit language into this [Chinese] language.
Section One: The Origin of the Dharma Assembly.
Thus have I heard.
"Thus" (*evam*) means that the ultimate truth does not contradict the conventional; it is called "thus" because the conventional accords with the ultimate. Therefore, it is termed "thus."
"Thus have I heard this Dharma from the Buddha. Here, "I" (aham) is Ānanda’s own designation; it means that when the Buddha preached this sutra, he personally heard it.
When this sutra speaks of "I," it refers to the true self that is characterized by emptiness and non-self.
"Those who hear" refers to the true hearing that is devoid of hearing based on emptiness. Formerly, a disciple frequently asked the Buddha:
"When the scriptures and teachings are compiled at a later time, how should they begin? The Buddha said: "They shall begin with 'Thus have I heard' (evam mayā śrutam)."
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
"At one time" refers to the occasion when the Buddha preached this sutra. "Buddha" means awakening. The essence of the mind is free from thought;

it awakens to and understands both the real and the false. The essence of awakening pervades the entire Dharma-realm and reaches the limits of empty space; it is the most pure of all. To be deluded regarding this—
When sentient beings awaken to this, they are Buddhas. Śrāvastī is the kingdom where King Prasenajit resided.
Jeta’s Grove refers to the trees donated by Prince Jeta; thus it is called Jeta’s Grove. Regarding the Anāthapiṇḍada Park:
in the kingdom of Śrāvastī there was an elder named Sudatta, who formerly served non-Buddhist [teachers].
He was also fond of giving alms and aiding the poor and the orphaned; therefore, the people of the country called him the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, his heart conceived a thirst for and yearning toward it.

He spread gold to purchase Prince Jeta’s garden and established a vihāra there, inviting the Buddha to reside therein and preach the Dharma. Because Jeta donated the trees and the Anāthapiṇḍada the garden, it is thus named.
It was at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. As for "the solitary" (anātha): one who is orphaned in youth is called "solitary" (gu), while one who is childless in old age is called "lonely" (du).
He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
"Bhikṣu" contains three meanings: first, a mendicant; second, one who destroys evil; and third, one who terrifies Māra.

"Mahābhikṣu" (Great Bhikṣu) is a title of honor for one's moral virtue and realization. Regarding the phrase "together with twelve hundred and fifty people": the Buddha first ordained the five men, including Cunda;
next, he ordained the three Kāśyapa brothers along with their disciples, numbering one thousand; and subsequently, he ordained Śāriputra...
Pūrṇa and Maudgalyāyana each led one hundred disciples. Next, they converted fifty people, including the elder Yaśas;
the sūtra cites this as a general figure, thus omitting five persons. This group had all previously served non-Buddhist teachers before subsequently receiving the Buddha’s teachings.
At that time, when it was the hour for eating, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

"At that time" refers to the occasion when he encountered the mealtime. "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) means that throughout successive lifetimes he has always looked up to as the sole Honored One of the three realms;
thus he is called the World-Honored One. "The hour for eating" refers to the time when people eat, at which point the Buddha donned his three [robes].
Wearing his robes and carrying his precious alms bowl, he entered the city to beg for food and to transform sentient beings. As for "entering the city" to remove arrogance:
since the monastery was outside the city, he entered from the exterior; therefore, it is called "entering the city."

Having finished his almsround through the city in due order, he returned to his original location. When he had finished his meal, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and sat down upon the prepared seat.
Regarding the sequence: without discriminating between the poor and the wealthy, he went for alms.
Upon arriving at his destination—the Jeta Grove Monastery—he set aside his three robes and his alms bowl.
Thereafter, having washed his feet, he sat down cross-legged.
Section Two: The Inquiry of Subhūti.

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti rose from his seat amidst the great assembly; he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying: “It is marvelous, World-Honored One!”
Subhūti, as a disciple of the Buddha, he practices and realizes the state of non-contention; thus he is called "Well-Appeared" (*Sujāta*).

Having realized that all phenomena are illusory and having awakened to the principle of true emptiness, he is also called "Born of Emptiness" (*Śūnyatājāta*) and "One Who Understands Emptiness" (*Śūnyatāvibodha*).

Venerable One, because his mind has attained the right path of Bodhi and he is named according to that principle, he is named Subhūti. He requests the Buddha to reveal and instruct him regarding the wondrous mind of Bodhi.
Therefore, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his knees on the ground, and joined his palms. He addressed the Buddha with reverence, saying: "This is the arrival of the teaching;

it is for the sake of reverence alone. How rare, O World-Honored One! By this, he meant that the Buddha’s merit and wisdom were both perfected. He praised him, saying that within the triple world, there is few who possess the compassionate pity of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; he skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas. "Tathāgata" is a title for the Buddha.

"Tathā" (Thus) refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), and "āgata" (Come) refers to initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*). Because the original and the initial are non-dual, one is called a Tathāgata.
"Bodhisattva" is a general term for those who practice the path. "Bodhisattva" is a Sanskrit term... [the word *bodhisattva*].
Regarding *tisaṭva*: for the sake of brevity, the text here uses the term "bodhisattva," which is translated as "enlightened sentient being" (*jue youqing*).

If within the nature of enlightenment there is the delusion of a sentient being, one is called a "sentient being" (*sattva*); if one is enlightened and free from the delusion of a sentient being, one is called a "Buddha.
Thus, "sentient being" (*youqing*) refers to a "living being" (*sattva*). Only the Tathāgata, out of his compassionate pity for sentient beings, is well able to maintain [this state].
[The Buddha] protected [them]. Possessing great wisdom, he entrusted the Dharma of the One Vehicle mind to the various Bodhisattvas.
"World-Honored One, how should good sons and good daughters who have resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi abide? How should they subdue their minds?"
*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is a term from the Sanskrit language; it is translated here as "Unsurpassed, Profound, Right, Equal, and Perfect Enlightenment.
This is precisely the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*yuanjue miaoxin*) inherent in human beings.
If a person gives rise to this mind of right enlightenment, upon what should they rely, and how can they subdue this deluded mind of dust?
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;
he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you.”
"Excellent, excellent! is a term of praise. It means that Subhūti is well able to inquire about this wondrous mind of bodhi.
"Dì" (諦) means to examine with precision.
Good sons and good daughters, you should give rise to the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"One should abide in this way; one should thus subdue the mind. "Yes, indeed, World-Honored One; I wish most earnestly to hear it.
"Should" (*yīng*) means "it ought to be so. "In this way" (*rúshì*) means "in accordance with principle," that is, as it truly is, without deviation.
This statement intends to bring forth the wondrous, pure, true mind of Bodhi. One ought to abide within the mind of Bodhi; only by doing so can one subdue [the mind].
"Vofenwangzhixin" (伏塵妄之心) means "to subdue the mind of delusive dust. "Wei" (唯) signifies "yes"; "ran" (然) signifies "so it is.

When Subhūti heard the Buddha speak these words, he was truly able to subdue his delusions and attained silent realization without doubt. His response, "Wei," was swift; he acknowledged the Honored One’s teaching and received its instruction.
"I wish to hear it with joy. "Joy" means love. ○ Third Division:
The True Source of the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner. Whatever..."
"Of all classes of sentient beings":
*mahā* is a Sanskrit term; here it means "great. A *mahāsattva* is thus a "Great Bodhisattva."
"All sentient beings. "All" is a general designation. "Beings" (zhòng) is a term for those who are not one. "Sentient" (shēng) carries the meaning of arising and ceasing.
Whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or lacking form; whether possessing perception... [and so forth].
Whether they possess perception, lack perception, or possess neither perception nor non-perception, I shall cause them all to enter Nirvana without remainder and bring them to liberation.
Although sentient beings are numerous, they do not exceed the nine types and twelve categories; yet within the essence of Nirvana, there are fundamentally no sentient beings.
According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is the luminosity of awakening that constitutes the fault. From the interaction of the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses, the nature of karma arises:

through the manifestation of light and form, seeing and luminosity give rise to perception; from divergent perceptions, hatred is formed; from concordant perceptions, attachment is formed; and this flowing attachment becomes the seed.

Taking thought as the embryo, through the union of intercourse, life is generated. Drawing in those of similar karma, six kinds of disordered thoughts arise according to one's karma, resulting in the birth of various sentient beings;
each species comprises eighty-four thousand varieties, filling their respective categories. As for those born from eggs, the egg arises solely from thought;
the union of vital energies forms the egg, and as consciousness and thought determine whether one flies or sinks, there are thus the classes of fish and birds.

Furthermore, as for those born from a womb (*jarāyu-ja*), the womb arises due to emotional attachment; the union of semen and blood forms the embryo. Because their desires and thoughts are either upright or horizontal, they are reborn among the species of humans and animals.
As for those born from moisture (*saṃsveda-ja*), moisture is produced through the stimulus of union; the blending of craving constitutes moisture, which, combined with warmth, brings about birth.

Their destination is not fixed, and because their thoughts are inverted and chaotic, they are reborn among the species of crawling insects and the like. As for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*)...

As for those born through transformation (*nirmāṇa*), they manifest by means of detachment from their physical bodies. Their minds desire to soar aloft, pursuing new and chaotic thoughts; thus, what was non-existent suddenly comes into being.
Hence, there exist classes of beings that undergo metamorphosis and fly through the air. As for those with form, they merely serve the sun, moon, and stars, stubbornly clinging to obstructive forms.
Their minds harbor chaotic thoughts that coalesce into spiritual radiance; these spirits of portents and omens abound in every direction.
If one belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one is weary of existence and clings to emptiness; the body is extinguished and returns to nothingness.

Delusion and karma are heavy and obscuring, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) attaches itself to the aggregates (*skandha*) and remains hidden. Its substance merges with the dullness of emptiness, and as that emptiness disperses and sinks away, those of this class fill the world.

If one belongs to the realm of perception (*saṃjñā*), one loses the truth through false imaginings and becomes perversely attached to reflected images; there is no actual form, yet one relies on consciousness to manifest a semblance, secretly forming appearances and shapes within the spirit.
There are ghostly spirits; their kind fills [the world]. Those who are "without thought" do not understand the principle of the Truths, stubbornly clinging to ignorance.

They practice meditation while harboring ashes of doubt, their contemplation becoming exclusively withered and parched. Their spirits transform into earth, wood, metal, and stone; their kind fills [the world].
As for those who are "not without thought," they deceive and misappropriate what belongs to others, claiming it as their own. They forget the ancestral sacrifices and offerings, yet they recognize...

That school’s lineage consists of those of differing natures who form one another; their kind fills [the world]. If they were not those who have attained the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñin*), they would repay enmity with enmity and respond to injury with killing;
their natural disposition would be strange and perverse, and they would cast aside the principles of human relations.

They would be like the earth-owl, which takes clods of earth as its offspring and becomes their parents, only to be devoured by them all; their kind fills [the world]. This explains the nine kinds and the twelve.

All such sentient beings have not yet awakened to the clarity of *nirvāṇa*. Their wondrous mind is lost in delusion, and their passions accumulate false imaginings, giving rise to a cycle of wandering through birth and death. Who among them does not know that the essence of the mind is fundamentally *nirvāṇa*?

If, for even a single thought-moment, they turn the light inward and awaken to the principle of non-arising, severing emotional delusions, they will immediately realize and enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
And thus one attains extinction by oneself. Nirvāṇa is precisely the mind that is without arising or ceasing. Within the realm of sentient beings, there is neither deficiency nor excess.
"With remainder" refers to when habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been exhausted; "without remainder" refers to when both subject and object have been entirely eliminated.
"In this way, he brings to parinirvāṇa immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, yet in reality there are no sentient beings who have attained parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span..."
That is not a bodhisattva. Regarding the four marks:

when the conscious mind has not yet attained realization, there is the mark of a self (*ātman*). When one is deluded regarding oneself and identifies with others, there is the mark of a person (*pudgala*).

When delusive emotions have not been eliminated, there is the mark of a sentient being (*sattva*). When there is a subsequent thought of existence, there is the mark of a life-span (*jīvita*). This is the mind of a bodhisattva.
Purity. All dharmas are unarisen; in reality, they possess no marks. If the four marks are removed, one is not a true Bodhisattva.
Chapter Four:
The Section on Sublime Practice Without Abiding.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice generosity without dwelling on anything at all regarding phenomena. That is to say, they should not dwell on form when practicing generosity;

they should not dwell on sound, odor, taste, tactile objects, or mental phenomena when practicing generosity. Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice generosity in this manner: without dwelling on signs.
"Furthermore" (*punar-aparam*) serves as a reiterative phrase. When the mind has dwelling and attachment, it is termed a mind of stinginess and greed;
when there is no dwelling or attachment, it is termed giving (*dāna*). "Dharma" is a name for the dust-like delusions; "giving" is the meaning of the Dharma of liberation.

Since the Dharma fundamentally has no place of abiding, arising and ceasing follow conditions. It is said that a Bodhisattva should not be attached to the mind, but should practice giving. [This concerns] the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
That which is in the eye is called form; in the ear, sound; in the nose, fragrance; in the tongue, flavor; in the body, touch;
and in the mind, phenomena. Now, regarding these characteristics of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), if one gives rise to defiled attachment, it constitutes stinginess and greed;
if there is no dwelling or attachment, it is termed giving (*dāna*).
Why is this? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, that merit cannot be measured or conceived.

One who gives without dwelling on signs is a bodhisattva whose awakened mind is pure; knowing that all phenomena are fundamentally empty, although they engage in the myriad practices to benefit sentient beings, they harbor not even a trace of attachment to the resulting merit. With a pure mind untainted by defilement, such is their merit.
"It is immeasurable.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the space of the eastern direction be measured? No, World-Honored One.
Subhūti, can the space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured? No."
[The sound "fu" (弗). World-Honored One, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices giving without abiding in signs, their merit is likewise immeasurable and inconceivable.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide in accordance with what has been taught.
East, south, west, and north constitute the four cardinal directions; the four intermediate points (catur-vidiś) are the four corners.

When these four cardinal directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir are taken together, they are collectively termed the ten directions (*daśa-diś*). Space (*ākāśa*) originally has no location or direction; how, then, could there be ten directions? The Buddha said:
"The ten directions" is a manifestation of the fact that this space is infinitely great. Now, it is said that the Bodhisattva arrays [offerings] without abiding in signs.
Regarding the statement that the merit of such giving is likewise as vast: if the mind encompasses the great void, then the nature of that merit is also equal to the vastness of the great void.
For this reason, the Buddha told the Bodhisattvas: "One should not dwell in dharmas or dwell in signs;
rather, one should dwell with a mind that has no place of dwelling. If the mind has no place of dwelling, this is called true dwelling."
Chapter Five: Seeing According to Reality as It Is.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his physical marks? “No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of his physical marks. Why is this? Because the so-called physical marks of the Tathāgata are...
It is not a physical form.
The Tathāgata is precisely the nature of True Suchness (tathatā). This is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) of all Buddhas, which is the fundamental essence of sentient beings.
As for "physical form," this refers to the illusory appearance of the form-body (rūpakāya). It is said that one cannot perceive the Truth by clinging to illusory appearances.
It is like the wondrous mind. Phenomenal marks are fundamentally illusory and empty; therefore, the Buddha said that the physical marks of the body are not physical marks.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever marks there may be, they are all false and delusive. If one perceives that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata."
If one perceives all marks as non-marks, the mind will not give rise to the conceptualizing thought of perceiving marks.
If one perceives marks and clings to marks, one turns away from the true principle; yet, by seeing that marks are non-marks, one sees the Tathāgata.
Chapter Six: The Rarity of Right Faith.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases as these, [will attain right faith]?”

“Will they give rise to true faith? The Buddha told Subhūti, “Do not speak thus. After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, who will be able to give rise to faith in these chapters and verses and regard them as true.
You should know that such persons have planted roots of goodness not under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas alone, but have already [planted them] under countless Buddhas.”

Having planted roots of goodness under millions of buddhas, those who possess true faith constitute the stairway to the ultimate truth. When there is faith, the principles of what is taught accord with reality; when they accord with reality, the way of teacher and disciple is perfected.
It was because Subhūti harbored doubts regarding this discourse by the Tathāgata on the chapter concerning the signlessness of *prajñā*.

[These] phrases are difficult for sentient beings to believe; therefore, they ask this question. However, the Buddha, fearing that he might obstruct the sentient beings' heart of true faith, first tells them not to speak thus:
"Let those who uphold the precepts do no evil; let those who cultivate merit practice all that is good.
If, after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, there are those who hear these chapters and verses of the Prajñāpāramitā and believe in them...
If they truly exist, one knows that such persons have not merely planted various roots of goodness before three or five Buddhas;
rather, throughout immeasurable kalpas, they have served all Buddhas and planted roots of goodness.
"Subhūti, as for those who hear these phrases and give rise to pure faith even for a single thought-moment, the Tathāgata knows them all and sees them all;
these sentient beings shall obtain such immeasurable merit. Why is this?

Because these sentient beings no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a being, or the notion of a life-span; they possess no notion of dharmas, nor do they possess the notion of non-dharmas."
"Pure faith": "pure" means pure and untainted; "faith" means believing without doubt.
If a person hears these phrases and gives rise to even a single thought of pure faith, one should know that this person’s mind is empty and the four marks and all phenomena are inherently pure.
"The mark of dharmas does not exist" means there is nothing to be grasped by views. "Nor does the mark of non-dharmas exist" means...
There is that which is grasped through views; thus, the characteristics of dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, yet they appear to exist due to the grasping of attachments.
If one can have pure faith, then the defilement and purity of sentient beings will be like this, and one shall immediately obtain immeasurable merit.
Why is this? If these sentient beings grasp at signs with their minds, they immediately become attached to a self, a person, a being, and a life-span.
If they grasp at the signs of dharmas, they likewise become attached to a self, a person, a being, and a life-span. Why is this? If they grasp at the signs of non-dharmas...
One would then be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. For this reason, one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas.
By this principle, the mind is fundamentally without marks. If one seeks the mind to grasp its marks, one is immediately attached to the four marks. This applies whether it be dharmas or non-dharmas.
All belong to delusive conditions and are entirely devoid of real characteristics. If one grasps at them and seeks them, one will likewise be defiled by the four marks.

Therefore, the essence of all dharmas is empty; one should not grasp or cling to them. For this reason, the Tathāgata taught that one should not grasp at marks. It is for this meaning that he spoke thus.
The Tathāgata has often said: "O bhikṣus, you should understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the parable of the raft.
Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."
The Buddha said: "All dharmas ferry me across; in all minds, there is no 'self. Of what use is any mind?
It is for this reason that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma. That which is like a boat or raft can ferry people from this shore to the other shore.

Since the four marks of persons are empty and the dust of the world is void, the mind is pure through the True Dharma; one should abandon even these, let alone what is not the Dharma. This is precisely what is meant.
When crossing a river, one should use a raft; once the shore is reached, the boat is no longer needed.
Chapter Seven: Neither Attainment nor Exposition.
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (the supreme, perfect enlightenment)?
"Devata, has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti replied, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught,
there is no fixed dharma named *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can preach."
The wondrous mind of the Tathāgata has no fixed dharma; this is precisely what is called bodhi. Furthermore, there is no fixed dharma that can be expounded.

Just as a mirror originally possesses no fixed images, yet they appear spontaneously according to forms, so too dharmas originally possess no fixed essence, yet they arise spontaneously according to conditions.
The *Daode jing* says: "Emptiness is emptiness; emptiness has no fixed emptiness. Form is form; form..."
This is the absence of fixed form.
Why is this so? All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and ineffable; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
Why is this? Because all worthy ones and sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Within the essence of the unconditioned, there is truly no dharma that can be apprehended or described. Now, when this sutra says "neither dharma nor non-dharma," it means that regarding this dharma, to say it exists is not to say it exists;
to say it does not exist is not to say it does not exist. As for "non-dharma," it is the original nature of the mind.
This "non-existence" is not a non-dharma; it exists through conditions. In principle, there is but the One Mind; in phenomena, it encompasses the myriad dharmas. Why is this so?
It is because while the principle is neither broad nor narrow, the depth of one's vision varies.

Upon this essence of the unconditioned, some may grasp the skin, some the bone, and some the marrow. The ranks of the sages and worthies are honored according to their merit; thus, those whose vision is deep advance in practice.
Extensive. Of high rank and eminent reputation, the worthy sages of the Three Vehicles realize awakening upon this essence of non-action (*asamskṛta*), each with varying degrees of depth.
○ Section Eight: Arising in Accordance with the Dharma.
Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? (Is it not so?)
Regarding the "trichiliocosm": the movement of the sun and moon around a single Mount Sumeru, illuminating the four continents, constitutes one small world-system (*cūḍika-lokadhātu*).
One thousand such small world-systems constitute one small chiliocosm (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*).
One thousand small chiliocosms constitute one medium chiliocosm (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*). One thousand medium chiliocosms constitute one... [great chiliocosm].

The "Great Trichiliocosm" refers to the total of one thousand great chiliocosms, one thousand middle chiliocosms, and one thousand small chiliocosms, which together constitute the Great Trichiliocosm.
As for the "seven treasures," they are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, agate, pearl, and crystal.
The Buddha said that one should give as an act of charity all the seven treasures throughout the Great Trichiliocosm. Thus he spoke.
Although the merit obtained is great, it does not equal the greatness of the merit of *prajñā*.
Subhūti said: "It is very much so, World-Honored One. Why is this? This merit is not the nature of merit;
therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great."
Subhūti has realized the Samādhi of Non-contention and awakened to the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
When he says that the merit is exceedingly great, his mind accords with non-contention; when he says it is not merit, his nature awakens to true emptiness.
The nature of merit is precisely the wisdom of Prajñā. Because the nature is not [conventional] merit, the Tathāgata speaks of the abundance of merit.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if there should be someone who receives, upholds, and even explains as little as a four-line verse from this sutra to others, their merit would surpass that [of the former]. Why is this?
Subhūti, all Buddhas and the Dharma of the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas—all emerge from this sutra.

Regarding the phrase "even as little as a four-line stanza" (*catus-pādikā gāthā*) in this sutra: do not merely say that the two characters "even as" (*nai-zhi*) appear above the term "four-line stanza" and the character "etc.
(*deng*) appears below it. It may consist of one line, two lines, or even hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, or millions of lines;
this is a general statement. Why, then, is it specifically called a "four-line stanza"? Those who read the sutra should examine this carefully.
This is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). These words provide a comprehensive exposition of the great meaning within the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The verse on the signlessness of *prajñā* speaks of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This means that the essence of the human mind is fundamentally unconditioned by nature;
one should rely upon *prajñā* to realize the fruit of the unconditioned. If a person can awaken to and clarify the true principle within this sūtra, they should direct their mind toward it.
If one further explains the meaning of this sutra for others, that person’s merit will surpass the merit of the previous three thousand sevenfold precious offerings.
Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang said: "Though three thousand sevenfold precious things are many, once used up, they return to birth and extinction;
though the four lines of the sutra text are few, if one awakens to them, one reaches directly to Bodhi. Thus it is said.
That all Buddhas and all Buddha-dharmas emerge from this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* indicates that this sutra alone is of the utmost importance.
Subhūti, what are called "Buddha" and "Dharma" are, in fact, not "Buddha" and "Dharma."
The Buddha-dharma resides in the mind and not in the teachings. Thus it is said: "That which is called the Buddha-dharma is not the true Buddha-dharma.
Chapter Nine:
The Section on One Appearance and Appearancelessness.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does a srotāpanna (one who has entered the stream) have this thought:
‘I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna’? Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A srotāpanna is called one who has entered the stream;
yet as for that which is entered, he does not enter into form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or dharmas. This is why he is called a srotāpanna.”
The Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat—these four fruits are the stages through which ordinary persons enter the ranks of the sages.
The mind of a person should take non-thought as its essence and non-attachment as its function.
The Buddha feared that people might harbor thoughts of these four fruits within themselves, which would sprout and obstruct their Way.
Therefore, these four fruits were established and questioned; Subhūti answered each with "No. He further engaged in a dialectical discussion:
if spoken of in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), there are fruits and characteristics; if spoken of in terms of principle (*tattva*), there are neither fruits nor characteristics.
By severing the three fetters, one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*; one does not fall into the three evil realms and returns seven times among humans and devas, [thereby] forever...

Having severed all sufferings and entered into nirvana, one is called a "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna). With the mind no longer entering the realms of the six sense-objects, one has for the first time entered the ground of the noble ones; this is named *srotāpanna*.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a sakṛdāgāmin have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A sakṛdāgāmin is so called because he returns once more;
yet in reality there is no coming or going. It is for this reason he is named a sakṛdāgāmin."
Having severed the three fetters and attenuated greed, hatred, and delusion, one attains the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner).

Permanently severing all suffering and joyfully realizing the unconditioned, such a person is called a "once-returner. Having been born once more in the heavens and once more in the human realm, they then attain nirvāṇa.
Although they are called "one who comes and goes," in reality there is no coming or going; this is what is meant by being a Sakṛdāgāmin.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Anāgāmin have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin'?

Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? An Anāgāmin is called 'one who does not come back,' yet in reality there is no such thing as 'not coming back. It is merely designated as 'Anāgāmin.'"

Having severed the lower five fetters, one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*. With the afflictions of views and thought severed, one is eternally liberated from the wheel of suffering and enters *nirvāṇa*;
thus one is called a "non-returner" (*anāgāmin*), meaning one does not return to take birth in the desire realm. Yet, in reality, there is no such thing as a non-returner;
for the mind has nothing to be attained and does not cling to the mark of non-returning.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Arhat have the thought: ‘I have attained the path of an Arhat’?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. “Why is that? Because, in reality, there is no dharma named ‘Arhat.
World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have the thought: ‘I have attained the path of an Arhat,’ he would thereby be attached.”
The self, the person, the sentient being, and the life-span;
the fruit of arhatship—these involve the eternal severance of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as all afflictions and the cycle of arising and ceasing, without remainder.
By means of completely pure conduct, one is established in the Dharma without defilement and shall not come again to receive birth within the three realms.

As for the Arhat, they realize that all dharmas are empty; yet if they harbor the thought of having attained the Way, their mind of "attainment" has not been eliminated, and they are thus attached to the four marks.
“World-Honored One, the Buddha has declared that I have attained the samādhi of non-contention and am foremost among men;
I am a foremost arhat free from desire. World-Honored One, I do not harbor such a thought as: ‘I am an arhat free from desire. World-Honored One...”
If I were to have this thought, "I have attained the path of Arhatship," the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
It is because Subhūti actually has nothing practiced that he is named Subhūti,
one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
"Non-contention" (araṇā) means to follow along without opposition. "Samādhi" is a Sanskrit term;
here it is translated as "right reception" (samyak-pratigraha), which refers to the mind not receiving a single dharma. "Araṇa" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "non-contention.

Subhūti, having departed from the three realms and desiring to realize the dharmas of the four fruits of arhatship, attained the samādhi of non-contention. He realized the true emptiness of reality; thus he was a person...
Among these, he is the foremost. Although he has realized these four stages of fruition (*phala*), his mind does not give rise to the thought that he has attained them.
If the mind were to entertain such a thought of attaining fruition, it would be contrary to the Path.

The Buddha would then not say that Subhūti practices the conduct of non-contention (*araṇā-vihāra*). In reality, there is nothing practiced; one awakens to the fact that the mind is unattainable. Although it is so said...
The practice of non-contention is likewise but a hollow name.
○ Chapter Ten: Adorning the Pure Land.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "What do you think? When the Tathāgata was formerly with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, was there any dharma [attained]?"
"Was there anything obtained? "No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he truly obtained nothing regarding the Dharma.
'Tathāgata' is a title by which a Buddha refers to himself. 'Dīpaṃkara Buddha' is none other than the teacher of Śākyamuni Buddha.
The Dharma is realized through the mind; how could it be obtained from without? To seal the mind with the mind—this is what is called 'obtaining'."
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. "And why is that?
To 'adorn a buddha-field' is not to adorn it; it is merely designated as 'adorning'."
As for the adornment of a bodhisattva, it consists of the six perfections and the myriad practices as their adornment.
As for the buddha-field, it is the field of the mind. The wondrous mind of true thusness is the pure land of all buddhas and the source of awakening for all sentient beings.
To simply realize the purity of the emptiness of phenomena is itself true adornment. As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "According as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure.
This purity of mind is precisely what constitutes adornment. If one performs acts of giving while clinging to marks, it is not adornment;
yet it is given the name "adornment" [only figuratively].
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on forms;
they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. They should give rise to their minds by dwelling nowhere at all.
Since the adornment of a Buddha-land consists in the purity of the mind, a bodhisattva should give rise to an unstained, pure mind;
they should not give rise to a mind of delusive thoughts regarding the six sense objects. The word "er" (而) serves as a conjunction linking what follows to what precedes it.
"One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere" means that if the mind is unstained and pure, the true mind will arise of its own accord.
It is like a scale pan that is empty; its needle naturally aligns itself.
Subhūti, it is as if there were a person whose body were as vast as Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think? Is this body great? Subhūti replied:
"Very great, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because the Buddha has said that what is called 'body' is not a body; it is merely a designation."
"Great body" refers to one who is honored by the multitude, such as a king. Mount Sumeru reaches upward to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and extends downward to the limits of Kunlun;
it is the sovereign mountain of the Sahā world, its greatness unsurpassed. The Buddha cited this as a simile.
[The Buddha] said by way of analogy: "Suppose there were a human body as large as Mount Sumeru; would it be considered large? Subhūti, complying without dissent, replied:
"It would be very large. [The Buddha continued: "Though Mount Sumeru is large, it does not fill empty space. Such is the greatness of the Dharmakāya."
It encompasses the great void. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The void is born within your own mind; it is like a fragment of cloud appearing within the vast clarity of space.
How much more so, then, that the world is born within the void, and Mount Sumeru dwells within that world—how could it be considered great?
Therefore, the Dharmakāya is without marks and is truly great, whereas Mount Sumeru possesses marks.
It is not to be considered great. Therefore, the Buddha says that what is not a body is called the "Great Body.
Chapter Eleven: The Superiority of Merit from Non-action.
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. What do you think? [If for each of those grains of sand there were a Ganges River...]
"How so? Are all those sands of the Ganges many? Subhūti replied, "They are very many, World-Honored One.
Even the Ganges rivers alone are already innumerable, let alone their sands."
Regarding the Ganges: outside the city of Śrāvastī there is a river named the Ganges.

The Buddha frequently used the sand within this river as a metaphor, saying that within the Ganges there are these immeasurable grains of sand, and there are even more immeasurable Ganges rivers than there are grains of sand. The sand within all these Ganges rivers—this is what is meant by "much."
It is indeed so, Subhūti.

I now speak to you in truth: if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who were to fill as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, the merit they would obtain would be great.
Subhūti replied, "Very much so, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti, "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family,
from within this sutra, were to receive, uphold, and even recite as little as a four-line verse for others,
the merit of this would surpass the former merit."
Even if one were to offer the seven treasures as many times as there are sands in the Ganges River, the resulting merit would not surpass that of the human and celestial realms.
However, if a person thoroughly investigates and clarifies the ultimate truth within this sutra, they will certainly realize the fruit of Bodhi.
Chapter Twelve: Honoring the True Teaching.

Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even so much as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place should be honored by all the world—gods, humans, and asuras—as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha.
"Wherever it is preached" refers to the places where the sutras are taught to people. "Stūpas" are the shrines that enshrine the Buddha’s śarīra;
they are temples that establish the sacred image of the Buddha. Therefore, humans, devas, and asuras offer worship there.
Now, one should know that at these places where the sutras are preached, all those in the human realm, the heavenly realm, and the asura realm [gather].
They offer worship with incense, flowers, banners, and canopies that surpass even the stupas and temples of the Buddhas.
Why is this? It is because all the Buddhas and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dharma of all the Buddhas emerge from this sutra. Therefore, humans and devas revere it in such a manner.
How much more so for anyone who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it.
Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma. Wherever this sutra is located, there is a Buddha, as well as his honored disciples.
If a person clarifies this wondrous meaning of Prajñā and understands that the mind can become a Buddha, upholding it in this way constitutes the accomplishment of the foremost and most rare Dharma.
Since all Buddhas realize enlightenment by relying upon Prajñā, it is said that wherever this sutra resides, there is a Buddha. If such a person can honor this [sutra]...
[Sūtra]. This is how one honors the disciples. ○ Chapter Thirteen:
Receiving and Upholding According to the Dharma.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what should this sūtra be named? How should we uphold it?"
"Uphold it. The Buddha told Subhūti: "The name of this sūtra is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
By this title, you should uphold it."
"Vajra" is a metaphor for *prajñā* (wisdom). This is the *dharmaprajñāpāramitā*; "Pāramitā" is a Sanskrit term, which in this [language] means "wisdom that has reached the other shore.
This was extracted from the title of the aforementioned scripture; the commentary is hereby concluded. Regarding the phrase "by these names":
this refers to the name of the *prajñā*, not the essence of true *prajñā*. Therefore, it speaks of the "name. You should revere it.
As for "upholding," one should rely upon the meaning to practice and uphold the teaching so that it may circulate.
Why is this? Subhūti, what the Buddha calls the *prajñāpāramitā* is not actually the *prajñāpāramitā*;
it is merely designated as the *prajñāpāramitā*.
All verbal expressions are devoid of substantial meaning. Because *prajñā* is signless, the Buddha said that what is called *prajñā* is not *prajñā*;
it is merely designated as *prajñā*.
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma? Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has nothing to say.
The Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; yet, because the essence of true suchness is pure, in reality there is no dharma that can be spoken.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many?
Subhūti replied, "Very many, World-Honored One. "Subhūti, those atoms which the Tathāgata has spoken of are not atoms;
they are called 'atoms. The world which the Tathāgata has spoken of is not a world; it is called 'a world.'"
The trichiliocosm does not exist outside the mind; all atoms depend entirely upon the earth.
Therefore, the world arises according to what is evoked by the karma of sentient beings' minds. When the minds of sentient beings are pure, the world is pure;

when the minds of sentient beings are defiled, the world is defiled. To realize that phenomena have no intrinsic substance is to see that they are not composed of atoms; to realize that appearances are illusory is to see their emptiness.
Thus, it is not a world. The Buddha’s mind is empty and quiescent; he contemplates that these atoms are unreal and that the world is not solid.
Therefore, he says there is no such thing as a dusty world, yet this is precisely what is called a "dusty world."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?
“No, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said:”
The thirty-two marks are, in fact, no-marks; this is what is called the "thirty-two marks.
Regarding these thirty-two marks: the Tathāgata, through thirty-two sublime practices, brought forth this retributive body of sublime marks.
Pure like lapis lazuli, transparent both within and without, although this retribution body is exceptionally sublime, it is likewise illusory and false, ultimately destined for destruction.
Therefore, it is said that non-characteristic is itself what is called characteristic.
Subhūti, if a son or daughter of good family were to give away their body and life as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River,
